newsitem.title: RUSSIA: One Russian bank spurs industry change.
newsitem.headline: One Russian bank spurs industry change.

text.p: Russian banks are being forced into a new era of corporate investment and partnership with foreigners by the government's new financial stability and a move by a major bank to break formerly close ranks.
"We are here at the birth of real banking in Russia -- getting money to enterprises," said CentreInvest Securities research chief James Fenkner.
Economic transparency is only spotty but it is clear that the interests of banks and the government are diverging.

Banks nurtured by the government have seen rules tighten on sales of state assets. They have also seen yields on domestic bonds, which may have accounted for most of their profits last year, plummet from 200 percent a year ago to under 20 percent.
"If they are not feeding at the government trough, they are going to have feed at another trough," Fenkner said.
Competition at privatisation auctions until recently was minimal.

But Russia's third largest bank by assets, Uneximbank said on Friday the state was ready to sign a deal allowing it to buy 38 percent of major metal producer Norilsk Nickel, weeks after it bought a $1.9 billion stake in telecom holding Svyazinvest.
News media controlled by other financial groups who wanted Svyazinvest have said the sales would ignite a banking war.
But the sales appear to be clearing final hurdles and the government is serious about raising privatisation revenues.
Uneximbank's bids for both Norilsk and Svyazinvest were sharply above bid minimums, landmarks after years of auctions which appeared dominated by back-room deals.

Brunswick brokerage banking analyst Boris Sinegubko said cash-poor Russian financial groups such as Uneximbank and rival Menatep, which owns the Yukos oil holding company, were being forced to look for foreign partners.
"It will be difficult for them to do reforms on their own. They need Western partners. Sooner or later there will be strategic alliances for both Norislk and Yukos, I think."

Uneximbank, which said before the Svyazinvest auction that it planned to raise $500 million toward the deal, bid $1.875 billion for the stake and brought in international partners including U.S. financier George Soros.
Uneximbank in mid-July launched a $200 million Eurobond, funds from which may have been used for the acquisitions.

Russian macroeconomics have improved in the last year, allowing the state to attract cheap credits abroad without relying on expensive domestic bonds that nurtured domestic banks and left the government economically vulnerable.
But increased financial transparency does not mean the Russian back room has closed, and a small group of bankers and politicians wield an enormous amount of power.

Uneximbank raised its bid for Norilsk after last minute talks, a government source said. But it suffered for its victory days later when First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais ordered state customs committee accounts moved to state banks.
Kommersant Daily newspaper estimated such accounts held by Uneximbank at 5.5 trillion roubles. An Uneximbank spokesman declined to comment on the figure.

"In this country you still have to cooperate with these people," said Sinegubko. He predicted pressure from bankers and politicians would stop Uneximbank from participating in major auctions, such as an upcoming sale of a stake in Rosneft oil holding company.

But the apparent rap on Uneximbank's knuckles only accelerated a general plan for government banks to take over lucrative government accounts from commercial banks. Most such accounts with commercial banks are slated to be closed by 1998.
Fenkner said the banks would begin to rush to equities, though, acquiring cheap shares and marketing them abrad.
"Russia is still so undervalued it is hard to quantify and banks are in the best position to buy."
--Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
